_README: Per-question INTERNAL escalation guide for the live examiner. Keyed by question number (matching oral_exam_questions_list.txt and molecule_map.json). 'probes' are progressively deeper escalation TARGETS (concepts to push toward, not phrasings to read out); 'misconception' is the common wrong idea to watch for and probe. This content is injected into the examiner prompt as non-disclosed guidance and must never be shown to the student. Questions absent from this file simply get no extra guidance. Currently populated for the Stoichiometry topic (Q1-10) as a reviewable template; extend topic-by-topic.

1.misconception: Thinking a small reagent shortfall has only a negligible or non-linear effect, or reasoning from mass shortfall without converting to moles via the balanced ratio.
probes: Quantify the proportionality: if the loaded NaN3 is ~10% short, what happens to the moles (and therefore volume) of N2 produced?
Write and balance the decomposition (2 NaN3 -> 2 Na + 3 N2) and use the mole ratio to relate moles of azide to moles of N2.
Connect moles of N2 to the inflated volume via the ideal gas law (V proportional to n at fixed T and P).
Surface the assumptions behind the strict proportionality: reaction goes to completion, fixed T and P.

2.misconception: Believing the assay measures protein directly, or that any nitrogen-containing additive inflates the reading equally regardless of its mass-percent nitrogen.
probes: Why is nitrogen used as a proxy for protein at all (a fixed nitrogen-to-protein conversion factor)?
Why is melamine's mass-percent nitrogen so high - reason from its formula (C3H6N6) and molar mass.
Estimate the effect: with a ~6.25 conversion factor, roughly how much apparent 'protein' does a gram of melamine fake?
What measurement would distinguish genuine protein nitrogen from melamine nitrogen?

3.misconception: Thinking a percent yield below 100% means atoms were destroyed, or conflating percent yield with purity or percent composition.
probes: Define percent yield (actual / theoretical x 100) and state what the 'theoretical' value assumes.
Distinguish the possible causes: incomplete reaction, competing side reactions, and physical losses - which lower the yield?
Reconcile with conservation of mass: if only 78% of the ethanol formed, where did the rest of the carbon go?
How could the brewer push the yield higher (drive the reaction further, suppress side products)?

4.misconception: Confusing amount of substance (moles) with concentration; assuming a correctly sized tablet gives the right concentration regardless of water volume.
probes: Why does the same tablet give a different ppm in pools of different size (c = n / V)?
Carry out the calculation: given the moles of HOCl released and the pool volume, find the concentration.
What happens to the free-chlorine concentration as water evaporates or is topped up (dilution)?
Separate the two quantities: which does the tablet fix (amount), and which does the pool set (volume), and how do they combine?

5.misconception: Identifying the leftover reactant as the limiting one, or assuming more charcoal is always better without considering excess-carbon contamination.
probes: When carbon is short, which species is limiting and which is left over?
Write the reduction (e.g. 2 Fe2O3 + 3 C -> 4 Fe + 3 CO2) and use the mole ratio.
Describe the product when carbon is limiting (unreduced oxide / slag) versus when carbon is in excess (carbon mixed into the iron).
How does the limiting reagent set the maximum mass of iron obtainable from a given charge?

6.misconception: Assuming that because both reagents are physically present the reaction must run fully; overlooking that an unreleased reagent does not participate.
probes: Why does releasing only part of the H2O2 make it the limiting reagent even though 'both reagents are present'?
Relate the moles of excited intermediate (and hence photons emitted) to the moles of limiting H2O2.
Would fully cracking the ampoule restore full brightness - and what else could still limit it?
Distinguish brightness (amount/rate of light) from how long the glow lasts.

7.misconception: Treating excess reagent as wasteful or as an error, and confusing the logic of a back-titration with a direct titration.
probes: Why must the analyte (ethanol) be completely consumed in a back-titration?
What is actually measured (the leftover dichromate), and how does that yield the ethanol amount by difference?
What goes wrong if dichromate is limiting (unreacted ethanol -> the alcohol content is underestimated)?
Use the redox stoichiometry (ethanol oxidized, Cr(VI) -> Cr(III)) to back-calculate the ethanol consumed.

8.misconception: Treating the carbon anode as an inert electrode/spectator rather than a consumed reactant tied stoichiometrically to the product.
probes: Why does consumption of the carbon anode stoichiometrically limit how much aluminum can be deposited?
Write the cell reaction (2 Al2O3 + 3 C -> 4 Al + 3 CO2) and state the C-to-Al mole ratio.
For a strong student: connect charge passed (Faraday's laws) to the moles of aluminum deposited.
Why must the anodes be replenished periodically for production to continue?

9.misconception: Confusing per-pass conversion with overall yield, or believing the unreacted feed is destroyed/lost rather than recoverable.
probes: Why does a 70% per-pass conversion leave 30% of the feed unreacted (not consumed)?
How does recycling the unreacted heptane raise the overall yield toward 100% over multiple passes?
Clearly distinguish per-pass conversion from cumulative overall yield.
Why is recycling preferred to discarding (feedstock cost, atom economy)?

10.misconception: Thinking the reaction keeps going as long as any reagent remains, and not linking the limiting reagent to the measurable signal (color change).
probes: Why is ethanol the limiting reagent here (small breath sample against a fixed amount of dichromate)?
Why does the color change stop once the ethanol is gone, even though dichromate remains?
Why is the degree of color change proportional to the ethanol present - the basis for quantifying it?
Identify which species is oxidized and which reduced, and why Cr(VI) -> Cr(III) produces the color change.
